claim: In four two-response experiments with deadline and load to block deliberation, correct logical answers were often given as the first, fast answer, so slow correction is not the main source of correct answers.
quote: Our key finding is that we frequently observe correct, logical responses as the first, immediate response.
title: Fast logic?: Examining the time course assumption of dual process theory
transfer: Router rule: when the first answer is fast and agreed across probes, accept it and spend no deliberation; deliberation is not a default fix.

claim: Repeating deliberation did not raise accuracy of later fast (intuitive) answers, and in a further study on Stroop and Flanker tasks correct final answers were often non-corrective, i.e. already right at first response.
authors: Raoelison, Keime, De Neys; Voudouri, Bago, Borst, De Neys
title: Think slow, then fast: does repeated deliberation boost intuitive reasoning? ; Voudouri et al. 2023 Stroop/Flanker extension
venue: Judgment and Decision Making / related journals
transfer: Do not expect a second thinking pass to improve the next fast answer; use passes only when a check can fail the first answer.

claim: The two-types dual-process framework is argued to lack empirical support, contradict known findings and be internally incoherent; defenders reply that the critique targets a premise not central to current theory.
authors: Melnikoff, Bargh; Pennycook et al. (reply); Melnikoff, Bargh 2023 BBS commentary
title: The Mythical Number Two (Trends in Cognitive Sciences) and replies
venue: Trends in Cognitive Sciences; Behavioral and Brain Sciences 46
transfer: Do not build the schema as two fixed modes; use graded signals (agreement, check result) instead of a System 1 or 2 label. PDF could not be read (binary); known from search summaries.

claim: De Neys replied to 34 BBS commentaries on his fast-and-slow target article, which indicates the field treats the strict fast then slow picture as still under active revision.
quote: The 34 commentaries on the target article span a broad range of interesting issues.
title: Further advancing fast-and-slow theorizing
transfer: none (context: treat dual-process as a design heuristic, not a law).

claim: Schooler, Ohlsson and Brooks (1993) found that thinking aloud hurt insight problems but not non-insight problems; this is the origin of the claim that verbal deliberation can hurt insight.
title: Thoughts beyond words: when language overshadows insight
transfer: Hypothesis: forced written reasoning may hurt tasks that need restructuring; test as a control arm.

claim: A direct test with 80 participants found no insight-specific effect of thinking aloud; verbalizing hurt spatial problems more than verbal ones, favouring the business-as-usual view over special-process.
quote: These results favoured the 'business as usual' view of insight problem solving
title: Verbalization and problem solving: insight and spatial factors
transfer: The harm of verbal thinking tracks the task being spatial, not insight as such: route spatial or perceptual items to non-verbal tools (code, grids).

claim: A 2025 J. Intelligence study (Macchi) is reported to replicate the lack of verbalization effects on insight problems; I could not open it (HTTP 403) and know it from a search summary only.
title: Verbalization and insight problem solving (J. Intell. version of record)
transfer: Weakens the claim that verbal reasoning steps universally harm insight.

claim: In 115 students, solving of insight and non-insight problems followed a typical analytic method consistent with business-as-usual, with a rarer exceptional strategy also seen; neither pure view wins.
quote: The results indicate a typical, analytic solution method consistent with the business-as-usual theory.
title: Insight problem solving is not that special, but business is not quite 'as usual'
transfer: Most solving is incremental search; keep a rare restructure step but do not make it the main path.

claim: A 2023 paper states the evidence that insight needs sudden representational change is inconclusive, since many insight measures rely on solvers' subjective report; Ohlsson himself suggested the suddenness may be an illusion of poor introspective access.
title: Tracing Cognitive Processes in Insight Problem Solving: Using GAMs and Change Point Analysis to Uncover Restructuring
transfer: Do not use a model's aha wording as a signal of restructuring; use an observable change in answer or representation.

claim: Khemlani and Johnson-Laird's meta-analysis of 12 theories of syllogistic inference found none gave an adequate account; mental-model theory has a counterexample-search parameter in mReasoner, but a 2001 critique argued reasoners often build a single model and do not falsify.
title: Theories of the syllogism: a meta-analysis
transfer: Counterexample hunt is supported but human use is partial; make it a triggered step with a run, not a universal step.

claim: Klahr and Dunbar's two-space model was extended by Schunn and Klahr to four spaces (adding data representation and paradigm spaces); I found no replication or critique of the children-versus-adult confirmation findings in this session.
title: A 4-Space Model of Scientific Discovery
transfer: Agent should keep separate stores for hypotheses, experiments and how data is represented. Gap: no critique found, search budget ran out.

claim: Across a meta-analysis of over 100 papers and 20 datasets on 14 models, chain of thought helps mainly on math and symbolic tasks; on MMLU it matches direct answering unless an equals sign is present.
authors: Sprague, Yin, Rodriguez, Jiang, Wadhwa, Singhal, Zhao, Ye, Mahowald, Durrett
title: To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
transfer: Gate step-by-step reasoning to symbolic or computable items; skip on commonsense and word puzzles.

claim: Chain of thought lowered model accuracy by up to 36.3 points (o1-preview vs GPT-4o) on tasks where verbal deliberation also hurts humans: implicit statistical learning, visual recognition, and classifying with exceptions; on three other such tasks CoT did not hurt.
authors: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths
title: Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
transfer: Direct human-to-model link: use cognitive findings on where deliberation hurts as a list of no-deliberation task classes in the router.

claim: LLMs cannot reliably fix their own reasoning without external feedback, and accuracy can fall after self-correction.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback
authors: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
transfer: Every doubt or revise step must be tied to a run, test or differing input.

claim: Reasoning models show accuracy collapse beyond a complexity threshold, reduce effort despite unused budget, and are beaten by standard models on low-complexity puzzles at equal compute.
quote: face a complete accuracy collapse beyond certain complexities
authors: Shojaee, Mirzadeh, Alizadeh, Horton, Bengio, Farajtabar
title: The Illusion of Thinking
transfer: Matches our ARC and word-puzzle result: easy items go to the plain path; estimate difficulty before choosing the heavy schema. Contested by critics; treat as one benchmark.

claim: Reasoning models spend large amounts of computation on trivial problems (the paper's example is 2+3), a first systematic study of overthinking.
quote: This paper presents the first comprehensive study on the prevalent issue of overthinking
authors: Chen, Xu, Liang, He, Pang, Yu, Song and others
title: Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
transfer: Cap thinking tokens for items the probe solves at once; stop at the first verified answer.

claim: Chain-of-thought gains on Blocksworld planning appear only with very specific prompts and deteriorate quickly as problem size grows, so they do not reflect learned general procedures.
quote: CoT's performance improvements do not stem from the model learning general algorithmic procedures via demonstrations.
title: Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning
transfer: Problem-space search steps must call an external checker or simulator for depth; do not trust prompted step-lists to scale.

claim: Biasing features (such as always labelling the answer (A)) made CoT accuracy drop by as much as 36% on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks, and explanations did not mention the bias.
quote: This causes accuracy to drop by as much as 36% on a suite of 13 tasks from BIG-Bench Hard.
title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
transfer: Shuffle option order and strip hints before critic and judge steps; written reasons are not evidence of the real cause.

claim: The face-recognition form of verbal overshadowing was supported by a large multi-lab replication (Alogna et al. 2014), while the insight form has mixed results; so the human grounding is task specific.
title: Registered Replication Report: Schooler and Engstler-Schooler (1990)
transfer: none directly; caution against generalizing the overshadowing claim to reasoning. Could not re-open (cookie page); from a search summary.

claim: Jones (2003) tested representational change theory against a progress-monitoring theory of insight; and Oellinger, Jones, Danek and Knoblich (2013) report eight-coin results consistent with representational change, so support exists but a rival account fits similar data.
title: Testing two cognitive theories of insight; Cognitive mechanisms of insight: the role of heuristics and representational change in solving the eight-coin problem
transfer: Progress monitoring (count steps toward the goal, switch strategy when progress stalls) is a simpler trigger for a representation change than a sudden-insight model.
